title: Corsano CardioWatch 287–2 algorithm recognizes a real-life ventricular-fibrillation arrest and collapse in post-processing; the patient's implanted defibrillator ended the arrest, and the wristband sent no alert
summary: In post-processing, the CardioWatch photoplethysmography algorithm detected cardiac arrest at 09:50:17 after loss of pulse in a cyclist; his implanted defibrillator ended it, and no alert was sent.
account: The arrest took place before 16 December 2025, when Resuscitation Plus received the case report; the paper gives no calendar date for the event. A 64-year-old man with heart failure, permanent atrial fibrillation and a secondary-prevention Biotronik implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) was wearing the CE-certified CardioWatch 287–2 (Corsano Health, The Hague). He wore it in the DETECT-3 study. After three weeks, while cycling alone, he developed monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT). It accelerated to ventricular fibrillation (VF) after an antitachycardia pacing burst. The ICD delivered a 40 J shock. He regained consciousness, cycled home, and was admitted for rhythm observation with a good recovery. The wristband's 32 Hz photoplethysmography and accelerometry data were exported afterwards. A Corsano Health data scientist blinded to the event ran them through the DETECT photoplethysmography algorithm. It detected cardiac arrest at 09:50:17 after loss of pulse. It ended the alert at 09:50:57 when pulsations returned. The group's fall-detection algorithm flagged the fall about 8–10 seconds after pulselessness. Edgar, Jansen, Pol, Pisters, van Royen and Bonnes of Radboud University Medical Center (with Rijnstate Hospital) reported the case in Resuscitation Plus on 29 January 2026. They report that it is the first real-life cardiac arrest captured by a wristband with cardiac-arrest detection. The authors state that the detection was retrospective. They state that the study collects data to measure false-positive rates for a future live system. The patient's survival is attributable to the ICD. The wristband changed nothing for him. In an accompanying editorial, Veigl and Billig, clinicians in St. Poelten and Aachen with no declared tie to the device, wrote that the case is the first real-world proof of concept; they add no data on the event. In its earlier DETECT-1a study the group reported 98% sensitivity in induced circulatory arrests. In the DETECT-2 study, published on 7 March 2026, the group describes a machine-learning fall detector built from healthy volunteers' simulated falls. The case report does not name the fall model that it used. In April 2026 the group reported external validation in 50 patients with induced VT or VF (DETECT-1b). In July 2026, in The Lancet Regional Health - Europe, the group reported 100% sensitivity (23 of 23) with one false positive in true non-shockable arrests after withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment. That paper describes the algorithm as rule-based. No main results of DETECT-3 or live alerting had been published by October 2026.
purpose: Built to detect out-of-hospital cardiac arrest from wrist photoplethysmography and accelerometry and, in future, alert emergency services. The retrospective detection demonstrates the first half of that purpose.

ai_role.statement: The pulse-loss detector was run afterwards on exported data by a blinded Corsano data scientist. It flagged the loss of pulse, and the fall detector flagged the collapse. The developers' own papers are the only full sources; an independent editorial restates the case without new data.

The paper gives no calendar date for the event. They report the first real-life cardiac arrest captured by a wristband with cardiac-arrest detection. A 64-year-old man with heart failure, permanent atrial fibrillation and a secondary-prevention Biotronik ICD was wearing the CE-certified CardioWatch 287–2 (Corsano Health, The Hague). He wore it in the DETECT-3 study. After three weeks, while cycling alone, he developed monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT). fields.account: The arrest took place before 16 December 2025, when Resuscitation Plus received the case report; the paper gives no calendar date for the event. A 64-year-old man with heart failure, permanent atrial fibrillation and a secondary-prevention Biotronik implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) was wearing the CE-certified CardioWatch 287–2 (Corsano Health, The Hague). He wore it in the DETECT-3 study. After three weeks, while cycling alone, he developed monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT). It accelerated to ventricular fibrillation (VF) after an antitachycardia pacing burst. The ICD delivered a 40 J shock. He regained consciousness, cycled home, and was admitted for rhythm observation with a good recovery. The wristband's 32 Hz photoplethysmography and accelerometry data were exported afterwards. A Corsano Health data scientist blinded to the event ran them through the DETECT photoplethysmography algorithm. It detected cardiac arrest at 09:50:17 after loss of pulse. It ended the alert at 09:50:57 when pulsations returned. The group's fall-detection algorithm flagged the fall about 8–10 seconds after pulselessness. Edgar, Jansen, Pol, Pisters, van Royen and Bonnes of Radboud University Medical Center (with Rijnstate Hospital) reported the case in Resuscitation Plus on 29 January 2026. They report that it is the first real-life cardiac arrest captured by a wristband with cardiac-arrest detection. The authors state that the detection was retrospective. They state that the study collects data to measure false-positive rates for a future live system. The patient's survival is attributable to the ICD. The wristband changed nothing for him. In an accompanying editorial, Veigl and Billig, clinicians in St. Poelten and Aachen with no declared tie to the device, wrote that the case is the first real-world proof of concept; they add no data on the event. In its earlier DETECT-1a study the group reported 98% sensitivity in induced circulatory arrests. In the DETECT-2 study, published on 7 March 2026, the group describes a machine-learning fall detector built from healthy volunteers' simulated falls. The case report does not name the fall model that it used. In April 2026 the group reported external validation in 50 patients with induced VT or VF (DETECT-1b). In July 2026, in The Lancet Regional Health - Europe, the group reported 100% sensitivity (23 of 23) with one false positive in true non-shockable arrests after withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment. That paper describes the algorithm as rule-based. No main results of DETECT-3 or live alerting had been published by October 2026.
